newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan regulators talk tough on offshore futures.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan regulators talk tough on offshore futures.

text.p: Taiwan regulators on Wednesday took a hard line on offshore Taiwan stock index futures being launched on Thursday in Singapore and Chicago, vowing to ferret out illegal trading by local investors.

"We will cooperate with the Investigation Bureau to investigate any illegal trading on the futures index," Securities and Exchange Commission futures department director Lo Chin-an told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"Any trading on unapproved financial instruments will be considered illegal, including Thursday's indexes," Lo said.

Lo's tough stance contrasted sharply with comments a day earlier by Finance Minister Paul Chiu, who said Taiwan regarded the offshore index contracts as positive even though regulators had yet to allow Taiwan investors to trade them.

The Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Singapore International Monetary Exchange, or SIMEX, both plan to launch Taiwan stock index-linked futures contracts within five minutes of each other on Thursday. San Francisco's Pacific Stock Exchange will launch Taiwan stock options later the same day.

Taiwan, playing for time to build its own local futures infrastructure, has stopped short of deeming the offshore rivals hostile but has withheld technical cooperation and refused to lift a ban on trading of the contracts by local investors.
Investors are expected to skirt the ban by opening underground offshore accounts and trading by telephone.

Pressure to end the ban is expected to surge on Thursday if the new contracts attract active interest, and especially if the lack of access inside Taiwan fuels capital outflows big enough to destabilise the currency, stock and capital markets.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has threatened to cut off access to stock price data crucial to their indexes, though commission chairman Lu Tung-ying has said it would not do so during an initial six-month observation period.

Futures department director Lo did not elaborate on how his agency or the national Investigation Bureau would monitor the offshore trading, but said the CME and SIMEX would be on what he called a commission watchlist.

Lo criticised the CME and SIMEX contracts, saying their relatively small lot size gave them the appearance of being more speculative than merely risk-hedging instruments aimed at individual investors rather than institutions.
Experts estimate Taiwan stock-index futures could fuel T$50 billion (US$1.8 billion) a month in first-year turnover.

Taiwan is planning its own futures exchange but parliament's prolonged bickering over several drafts of an enabling Futures Trading Law has forced promoters to postpone the launch to 1998 from the second half of 1997.
Taiwan brokers said the futures being launched on Thursday would make the local stock market more volatile at the outset but in the longer term would become an important price factor.
Volumes on the SIMEX and CME contracts should be relatively low until Taiwan investors gain legal access, brokers said.
